title: English Tenses in Depth
description: Master the full range of English tenses at B1 level, from the present perfect to future forms and the past perfect. This course is designed for learners who have completed A2 and want to use tenses accurately in both speaking and writing.

topics.title: Module 1: Present Perfect vs Past Simple

lessons.title: How to Form the Present Perfect

content.content: {"time":1700000001000,"blocks":[{"id":"aB1cD2eF3g","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"The present perfect is formed with have/has + past participle. It connects the past to the present moment."}},{"id":"hI4jK5lM6n","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["I have visited Paris. (at some unspecified time before now)","She has finished her homework. (recently, and it matters now)","They have never eaten sushi. (life experience)"]}},{"id":"oP7qR8sT9u","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Use the present perfect for:"}},{"id":"vW0xY1zA2b","type":"list","data":{"style":"ordered","items":["Life experiences — Have you ever been to London?","Recent actions with present results — I've lost my keys. (I don't have them now)","Actions that started in the past and continue — She's lived here for ten years.","Actions in an unfinished time period — I've drunk three cups of coffee today."]}},{"id":"cC3dD4eE5f","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Key time expressions: ever, never, just, already, yet, for, since, recently, so far, this week/month/year."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.content: {"time":1700000002000,"blocks":[{"id":"fF6gG7hH8i","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Two of the most important uses of the present perfect are expressing life experience and duration."}},{"id":"jJ9kK0lL1m","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Experience: Use the present perfect to talk about things that happened at an unspecified time in your life. The exact time does not matter — what matters is the experience itself."}},{"id":"nN2oO3pP4q","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["Have you ever climbed a mountain?","I've never broken a bone.","She's been to over twenty countries."]}},{"id":"rR5sS6tT7u","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Duration with FOR and SINCE:"}},{"id":"vV8wW9xX0y","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["Use for + a period of time: for two years, for a long time, for ages","Use since + a point in time: since 2010, since Monday, since I was a child"]}},{"id":"zA1bB2cC3d","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Examples: I have known him for fifteen years. / We have lived here since 2018."}},{"id":"dD4eE5fF6g","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Common error: Do not use the past simple for unfinished situations. Say 'I have worked here for three years' (I still work here), NOT 'I worked here for three years' (which means you no longer work there)."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.text: I have known him for fifteen years. We have lived here since 2018.

subtopics.title: 1.2 Contrasting Present Perfect and Past Simple

lessons.title: When to Use Past Simple Instead

content.content: {"time":1700000003000,"blocks":[{"id":"gG7hH8iI9j","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"The past simple and present perfect are often confused. Here is the key difference:"}},{"id":"kK0lL1mM2n","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["Past simple — used when the time is known, specified, or finished: I saw that film last week. She graduated in 2019.","Present perfect — used when the time is not specified or the action is connected to now: I've seen that film. She has graduated."]}},{"id":"oO3pP4qQ5r","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"With past simple, you must use a finished time expression: yesterday, last year, in 2010, two days ago, when I was young."}},{"id":"sS6tT7uU8v","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Typical patterns:"}},{"id":"wW9xX0yY1z","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["'Did you ever try...?' is sometimes used informally, but 'Have you ever tried...?' is the standard B1 form.","When someone says 'I've just heard some news', the follow-up question is often in the past simple: 'Really? What did they say?'"]}},{"id":"aA2bB3cC4d","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"This switch from present perfect to past simple is very natural in English conversation."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.text: I visited Rome last summer. She has visited Rome three times.

subtopics.title: 2.1 Forming and Using the Past Perfect

lessons.title: The Past Perfect: Actions Before the Past

content.content: {"time":1700000004000,"blocks":[{"id":"eE5fF6gG7h","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"The past perfect is formed with had + past participle and is used to show that one past action happened before another past action."}},{"id":"hH8iI9jJ0k","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Think of it as the 'past of the past'. When you are already talking about the past and need to refer to something even earlier, use the past perfect."}},{"id":"kK1lL2mM3n","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["When I arrived at the station, the train had already left. (The train leaving = earlier event)","She had studied French for three years before she moved to Paris.","He didn't recognise her because he hadn't seen her for twenty years."]}},{"id":"nN4oO5pP6q","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Common linking words used with past perfect:"}},{"id":"qQ7rR8sS9t","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["by the time, after, before, when, already, never, just, because"]}},{"id":"uU0vV1wW2x","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Past perfect vs past simple: If the order of events is clear from before or after, the past simple can be used: 'After she finished work, she went home.' But the past perfect makes the sequence explicit and is more common in formal writing."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.text: By the time we arrived at the party, most people had already left.

lessons.title: Predictions and Decisions: Will and Going To

content.content: {"time":1700000005000,"blocks":[{"id":"xX3yY4zA5b","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"English has several ways to talk about the future. At B1 level, it is essential to understand the difference between will, going to, and present continuous for future."}},{"id":"bB6cC7dD8e","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"WILL is used for:"}},{"id":"eE9fF0gG1h","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["Spontaneous decisions made at the moment of speaking: 'I'll have the pasta, please.'","Predictions based on opinion or belief: 'I think it will rain tomorrow.'","Promises and offers: 'I'll help you with that.'"]}},{"id":"hH2iI3jJ4k","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"GOING TO is used for:"}},{"id":"kK5lL6mM7n","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["Plans and intentions decided before the moment of speaking: 'We're going to visit my parents this weekend.'","Predictions based on present evidence: 'Look at those clouds — it's going to rain.'"]}},{"id":"nN8oO9pP0q","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"PRESENT CONTINUOUS for future is used for:"}},{"id":"qQ1rR2sS3t","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["Fixed arrangements (like diary entries): 'I'm meeting the doctor on Tuesday.'"]}},{"id":"tT4uU5vV6w","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"The key distinction: will = spontaneous/opinion; going to = pre-planned/evidence."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

lessons.title: Advanced Future: Future Continuous and Future Perfect

content.content: {"time":1700000006000,"blocks":[{"id":"wW7xX8yY9z","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Two more future forms give you greater precision when speaking about the future."}},{"id":"aA0bB1cC2d","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Future Continuous (will be + -ing): Used for actions that will be in progress at a specific future time."}},{"id":"dD3eE4fF5g","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["At 8 o'clock tomorrow, I will be driving to work.","This time next week, we will be lying on a beach."]}},{"id":"gG6hH7iI8j","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Future Perfect (will have + past participle): Used for actions that will be completed before a specific future time."}},{"id":"jJ9kK0lL1m","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["By the end of the year, she will have saved enough money for a car.","By the time you arrive, I will have finished cooking."]}},{"id":"mM2nN3oO4p","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Typical markers:"}},{"id":"pP5qQ6rR7s","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["Future continuous: at this time tomorrow, this time next week, at 6 pm on Friday","Future perfect: by (the time), by the end of, before"]}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.text: By the end of the year, she will have saved enough money. At 8 o'clock tomorrow, I will be driving to work.
By the time you read this letter, I [will have already left] the country. At midnight on New Year's Eve, we [will be celebrating] with our friends. By next June, she [will have completed] her degree.

lessons.title: Past Continuous: Background and Interrupted Actions

content.content: {"time":1700000007000,"blocks":[{"id":"sS8tT9uU0v","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"The past continuous (was/were + -ing) is used to describe:"}},{"id":"vV1wW2xX3y","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["An action in progress at a specific time in the past: At 9 pm last night, I was watching TV.","A background action interrupted by a shorter action (past simple): I was walking home when it started raining.","Two simultaneous past actions: While she was cooking, he was setting the table."]}},{"id":"yY4zA5bB6c","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Structure with 'when' and 'while':"}},{"id":"cC7dD8eE9f","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["When + past simple (short action) — while + past continuous (longer background action)","'She was reading a book when the lights went out.'","'While I was studying, my phone kept ringing.'"]}},{"id":"fF0gG1hH2i","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Stative verbs (know, believe, want, like, own, seem) are NOT normally used in continuous forms: Say 'I knew the answer' not 'I was knowing the answer.'"}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.text: I was reading a fascinating book when my friend called.

content.targetPhrase: While they were having lunch, it suddenly started to snow.

content.text: I [was reading] a fascinating book when my friend called. While they [were having] lunch, it suddenly started to snow. At 10 o'clock yesterday morning, she [was presenting] her project to the board.

topics.title: Module 5: Time Expressions and Tense Combinations

lessons.title: Tense Timeline: Putting It All Together

content.content: {"time":1700000008000,"blocks":[{"id":"iI3jJ4kK5l","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"At B1 level, you should be able to use multiple tenses in a single piece of writing or conversation. Here is a summary of which tense to use at each 'time layer':"}},{"id":"lL6mM7nN8o","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["Past Perfect — Before another past event: She had eaten before he arrived.","Past Simple — Completed past event: He arrived at 7.","Past Continuous — Background/interrupted past: It was raining when he arrived.","Present Perfect — Past with present relevance: I've just heard the news.","Present Simple — Facts/habits/routines: She works downtown.","Future (will/going to) — Predictions/plans: They're going to move soon."]}},{"id":"oO9pP0qQ1r","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"When telling a story, you typically use: past continuous (background) + past simple (events) + past perfect (earlier events)."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.text: I had already finished dinner when she called, so we went for a walk instead.

lessons.title: Real Conditions: Zero and First Conditional

content.content: {"time":1700000009000,"blocks":[{"id":"rR2sS3tT4u","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Conditionals connect tenses in specific patterns. The zero conditional uses present + present and the first conditional uses present + will."}},{"id":"uU5vV6wW7x","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Zero Conditional — General truths, scientific facts, habitual results:"}},{"id":"xX8yY9zA0b","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.","If I drink coffee after 6 pm, I can't sleep."]}},{"id":"bB1cC2dD3e","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"First Conditional — Real, possible future situations:"}},{"id":"eE4fF5gG6h","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.","She will fail the exam if she doesn't study harder."]}},{"id":"hH7iI8jJ9k","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Important notes:"}},{"id":"kK0lL1mM2n","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["Never use 'will' in the if-clause: NOT 'If it will rain' → 'If it rains'","You can use 'unless' instead of 'if...not': 'Unless she studies, she'll fail.'","You can also use 'when', 'as soon as', 'before', 'after' + present simple for the future."]}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.content: {"time":1700000010000,"blocks":[{"id":"nN3oO4pP5q","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"The second conditional is used to talk about imaginary, hypothetical, or unlikely present/future situations."}},{"id":"qQ6rR7sS8t","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Form: If + past simple, would + infinitive"}},{"id":"tT9uU0vV1w","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["If I had more time, I would learn the guitar. (I don't have much time — imaginary)","What would you do if you won the lottery? (very unlikely or hypothetical)","If she spoke Italian, she could work in Rome."]}},{"id":"wW2xX3yY4z","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Was or were? In formal English and writing, use 'were' for all persons in the if-clause of the second conditional:"}},{"id":"zA5bB6cC7d","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["If I were you, I wouldn't do that.","If she were taller, she could be a model."]}},{"id":"dD8eE9fF0g","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"In informal spoken English, 'was' is also common with I/he/she/it."}},{"id":"gG1hH2iI3j","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Contrast with first conditional:"}},{"id":"jJ4kK5lL6m","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["First: If I have time, I will call you. (probable — I probably have time)","Second: If I had time, I would call you. (hypothetical — I probably don't have time)"]}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.content: {"time":1700000011000,"blocks":[{"id":"mM7nN8oO9p","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"One of the best ways to practise tenses is through storytelling. In English narrative writing, you typically use a combination of:"}},{"id":"pP0qQ1rR2s","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["Past simple — for the main events of the story","Past continuous — for background setting and interrupted actions","Past perfect — for events that happened before the main narrative"]}},{"id":"sS3tT4uU5v","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Read this example: 'It was a cold January morning. Snow was falling softly outside the window. Maria sat down at her desk and opened her laptop. She had been working on the project for three weeks, but something still wasn't right. She had promised her boss she would deliver it by Friday...'"}},{"id":"vV6wW7xX8y","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Notice how the tenses work together to create depth, show timing, and set the scene."}}],"version":"2.31.4"}
